reference.source: Braddom's Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation / pain medicine references
clinicalPearls: Presents as regional pain that is disproportionate in severity and duration to the inciting event, often following a fracture, sprain, surgery, or immobilisation of a limb

The diagnosis is clinical and rests on the Budapest criteria, requiring symptoms and signs across sensory, vasomotor, sudomotor/oedema, and motor/trophic domains with no better alternative explanation
Type I follows tissue injury without a defined nerve lesion, whereas type II (causalgia) follows an identifiable peripheral nerve injury
Characteristic features include allodynia, hyperalgesia, temperature and colour asymmetry between limbs, sweating changes, swelling, and later trophic changes to skin, hair, and nails

Early mobilisation and functional restoration through physical and occupational therapy are the cornerstone of treatment, with pain control used to enable participation in rehabilitation rather than as an end in itself
Graded motor imagery and mirror therapy can help address the cortical remapping and body-perception disturbances seen in the condition

Pharmacological principles favour agents targeting neuropathic pain such as gabapentinoids and certain antidepressants, alongside bisphosphonates and short courses of corticosteroids in selected early cases
Sympathetic nerve blocks and, in refractory cases, spinal cord stimulation may be considered as part of a multidisciplinary programme
Untreated or under-treated disease can progress to fixed contractures, disuse atrophy, and permanent functional loss, so timely recognition matters
reference.pathophysiology: Complex regional pain syndrome is a maladaptive response to injury involving several overlapping mechanisms. Peripheral and central sensitisation amplify nociceptive signalling, while neurogenic inflammation driven by neuropeptide release produces oedema, vasodilation, and warmth. Autonomic dysregulation causes vasomotor and sudomotor changes, and cortical reorganisation of the somatosensory and motor maps contributes to distorted body perception, motor dysfunction, and persistent pain. An exaggerated inflammatory and immune response, together with possible autoimmune contributions, is thought to perpetuate the disorder beyond the expected healing time of the original injury.
additionalDifferentials: Peripheral neuropathy or specific peripheral nerve injury
Vascular insufficiency or thoracic outlet syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment against the Budapest diagnostic criteria as the primary basis for diagnosis
Plain radiographs, which may show patchy periarticular osteopenia in established disease
Three-phase bone scintigraphy showing periarticular uptake in supportive cases
Quantitative sensory testing and infrared thermography to document sensory and temperature asymmetry
Investigations to exclude mimics, including venous Doppler, inflammatory markers, and nerve conduction studies where a nerve lesion is suspected
redFlags: Rapidly spreading swelling, erythema, or systemic features suggesting infection or deep vein thrombosis rather than CRPS
Progressive fixed contracture or dystonia threatening irreversible loss of limb function
Signs of compartment syndrome in an acutely painful, tense limb
Severe refractory pain with escalating opioid use and psychological deterioration
New or evolving focal neurological deficit implying an untreated nerve or spinal lesion
reference.prognosis: Outcomes vary widely; many patients improve substantially with early diagnosis and active functional rehabilitation, but a minority develop chronic, treatment-resistant disease with lasting pain, stiffness, and disability. Delay in diagnosis, prolonged immobilisation, and untreated psychological distress are associated with poorer recovery.
pitfalls: Prolonged immobilisation or splinting of the affected limb, which worsens stiffness and reinforces disuse
Delaying the diagnosis by attributing persistent disproportionate pain to the original injury alone
Focusing on pain elimination with escalating medication instead of restoring function through active therapy
Overlooking coexisting anxiety, depression, or catastrophising that undermine rehabilitation
Relying on imaging to confirm the diagnosis when the criteria are fundamentally clinical
